title: Adab of knowledge
hookLine: a stranger in white sits knee to knee with the Prophet and teaches by asking

cards: 'Umar ibn al-Khattab tells it, in Sahih Muslim. They were sitting with the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, when a man walked in. Very white clothes.

Very black hair. No dust of travel on him, and nobody there knew who he was. He sat right in front of the Prophet, rested his knees against the Prophet's knees, laid his palms on his thighs, and began to ask questions.
Only later did the Prophet tell them who it was. Jibril, the angel, come to teach them their religion. He taught by asking.

teach.h: A TEACHER WHO CAME AS A STUDENT.
teach.b: That scene holds the adab of knowledge in its posture. Jibril came to teach, and he came looking like a student. He sat close.
He was still. He asked, and listened. Respect for the one you learn from isn't flattery; it's how you sit.
The Qur'an shows the same with a prophet. In al-Kahf, Moses meets a servant of Allah who has knowledge he doesn't, a man tradition calls al-Khidr.

And Moses, himself a prophet, asks, in paraphrase: may I follow you, so that you can teach me some of the right guidance you've been taught? He's told he'll need patience. He agrees, and then struggles to keep quiet.

teach.h: MY LORD, INCREASE ME IN KNOWLEDGE.
teach.b: In Ta Ha, the Prophet himself is told to ask for more, in Pickthall's translation: "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge." Nobody in these passages has finished learning. Then the sharp piece.
Al-Saff, Pickthall again: "O ye who believe! Why say ye that which ye do not?"

teach.h: WHAT DID YOU DO WITH IT?
teach.b: And a hadith in al-Tirmidhi says, in paraphrase, that on the Day of Rising a person's feet won't move until they're asked about their life, their wealth, their body, and their knowledge: what did you do with it?
Not how much did you know. Knowledge, in this adab, isn't a collection. It's a debt paid in action.

how: Muslim students are taught to honor their teachers, to recite "My Lord! Increase me in knowledge," and to treat knowledge as something to act on, citing the hadith of Jibril and the hadith of what a person did with what they knew.

o: memorizing as many texts as you possibly can
never questioning or asking a teacher anything
honor the teacher, ask for more, act on what you know

games.q: the adab of knowledge — tap the pairs.
p: sat knee to knee and asked
asked to follow and be taught
why say ye that which ye do not?

s: in the hadith of Jibril, the angel came giving a lecture
he came as a questioner, sat knee to knee with the Prophet, and asked.
the Qur'an tells the Prophet to ask for more knowledge
Ta Ha: my Lord! increase me in knowledge.
in the hadith, a person is asked only how much they knew
the question in al-Tirmidhi is about knowledge: what did you do with it?

games.q: you're Moses, a prophet, and you meet a man with knowledge you don't have. what do you do?
o: teach him what you know first.
ask if you may follow him and learn.
walk on; you're already a prophet.
games.why: in al-Kahf, Moses asks to follow and be taught, and is told he'll need patience.

practice: Look back over these last days, the kindlier word, the near side of the dish, leaving room, honoring the guest, the line before a trip, the last word before sleep, or anything else you've learned lately.
Pick one you've heard and haven't yet done, and see exactly when it could happen. If you pray, you can say the line from Ta Ha: my Lord, increase me in knowledge.

wordCard.voice: Adab of knowledge. The manners of learning: honor the one who teaches, stay humble enough to ask for more, and act on what you know. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: knowledge; it begins with the throat letter 'ayn.

carryVoice: Your line: learn, then do. Knowing is the start, not the finish. Same time tomorrow.
